1.label: CDI bulletin 2025-2
1.title: California Department of Insurance, Bulletin 2025-2, wildfire consumer protections
1.notes: For a covered total loss in a state of emergency: if you ask, your insurer must advance at least four months of additional living expenses (ALE), with more paid on proof afterward. The FAIR Plan uses the term Fair Rental Value with the same four-month advance. For a furnished primary home that is a total loss, insurers must offer a contents payment of at least 30% of the dwelling limit, up to $250,000, without an itemized inventory; you can claim more later up to your contents limit. ALE lasts at least 24 months after a state of emergency, plus 12 months if rebuilding is delayed by circumstances beyond your control, plus six-month extensions for good cause, though dollar limits in the policy may run out first. If you rebuild or buy elsewhere you are owed the benefits you would have received rebuilding at the original site, capped at the cost to rebuild there, and the insurer cannot deduct land value. You have at least 36 months from the first actual cash value payment to collect full replacement cost, with six-month extensions for good cause. If the dwelling limit is not enough to rebuild, you may combine dwelling and other-structure limits up to the aggregate limit. After a total loss the insurer must offer to renew for at least the next two renewal periods.

2.label: CDI wildfire page
2.title: California Department of Insurance, wildfire resources
2.notes: Start by contacting your insurance company or agent and work with your adjuster toward a settlement you believe is fair and matches your coverage. If you are considering a public adjuster, take your time and check that the person is licensed and in good standing. The department has a tool to search for a residential policy after a declared disaster. A one-year moratorium on non-renewals applies to wildfire-affected policyholders. For questions about your insurance or a dispute with your insurer, call the department hotline at 1-800-927-4357 or use its hotline chat. Local Assistance Centers offer in-person help.

3.label: CDI smoke damage order
3.title: California Department of Insurance press release on smoke damage claims, March 7, 2025
3.notes: The Insurance Commissioner directed insurers to fully investigate all smoke damage claims and ensure fair payments, and not to deny them outright. People whose homes are uninhabitable, even without wildfire damage, could have coverage under ALE. For help call the department at 1-800-927-4357. To check a contractor’s license, the Contractors State License Board is at 1-800-321-2752 or cslb.ca.gov.

4.label: FEMA
4.title: FEMA fact sheet, assistance for survivors with insurance coverage
4.notes: If you have insurance and want FEMA disaster assistance, file a claim with your insurance company first. By law FEMA cannot duplicate benefits for losses insurance covers, so FEMA can only help with needs insurance does not cover. When you apply you must tell FEMA about all your insurance coverage. You can apply at DisasterAssistance.gov, with the FEMA app, or by calling 1-800-621-3362, and you can upload documents to your account.

5.label: Cal OES
5.title: Cal OES, what to do if your property is damaged or destroyed in a wildfire
5.notes: Contact your insurance company first, since insurance delivers the majority of financial help after disasters. For losses insurance does not cover, you can register for disaster assistance online at disasterassistance.gov, with the FEMA app, or by calling 800-621-3362.

6.label: CDI complaints
6.title: California Department of Insurance alert urging wildfire survivors to file formal complaints
6.notes: The Insurance Commissioner urged wildfire survivors facing delayed payments, claim disputes, multiple adjusters, smoke damage problems or other issues to file a formal complaint with the department. The department said a formal complaint is needed for it to take action and advocate for consumers.

7.label: Consumer Federation of America
7.title: Consumer Federation of America, California wildfire insurance one-pager
7.notes: Document the damage thoroughly with photos and videos, but only if it is safe. Do not enter unsafe areas. Keep damaged items until they have been documented.

8.label: United Policyholders
8.title: United Policyholders, filing an insurance claim for fire damage in California
8.notes: Fires that damage but do not completely destroy a home create their own claim issues. Watch for hidden damage from water, smoke, ash and mold.

9.label: CDI SB 495 release
9.title: California Department of Insurance press release on SB 495, contents payments without a list
9.notes: Beginning January 2026, when a policyholder has a total loss in a declared emergency, insurance companies are required to pay 60 percent of personal property (contents) coverage limits, up to $350,000, without requiring a detailed inventory. Consumers can call 1-800-927-4357 with questions or use the department website or online chat.

10.label: CDI claim rights
10.title: California Department of Insurance, your rights under the Fair Claims Settlement Practices Regulations
10.notes: Under California’s Fair Claims Settlement Practices Regulations, an insurer must acknowledge a claim within 15 calendar days and begin investigating, and must accept or deny the claim no later than 40 days after receiving proof of claim. The department’s booklet is written for auto claims, but it describes the duties these regulations place on insurers generally.

11.label: CDI living expenses
11.title: California Department of Insurance, insurance coverage for additional living expenses if the home is not habitable due to a wildfire
11.notes: Additional living expense (ALE), also called loss of use or fair rental value, covers extra costs when a home is not safe to live in because of a covered peril such as wildfire. Keep bills and receipts for relocation costs such as hotel, clothing and food. Most renters insurance policies cover ALE only until you can move back or have had a reasonable time to find a rental elsewhere, whichever is less, so renters may not get the full length of time that homeowners get. Even a home with no damage may qualify if hazards make it unsafe and the policy provides ALE. For smoke and ash toxins from neighboring properties, the policyholder may need to show the home is uninhabitable, and the insurer should investigate and test.

12.label: United Policyholders wildfire page
12.title: United Policyholders, 2025 California wildfires insurance claim and recovery help
12.notes: United Policyholders’ page for the 2025 California wildfires collects orientation videos, a guide to reading your policy, videos on living-expense coverage for total losses and for standing homes, sample letters to request information about living-expense benefits and to request extensions, renters insurance claim tips for California, an insurance accounting spreadsheet, and a guide to speaking up when communicating with your insurer. It advises asking for the advance payments in writing; email counts.

13.label: LA County tenant guide
13.title: Los Angeles County Department of Consumer and Business Affairs, after the disaster, information for landlords and tenants
13.notes: If a rental unit is completely destroyed in a disaster, the lease no longer applies, rent is no longer owed and the landlord need not provide housing; the landlord must return prepaid rent and refund the security deposit under California law. If a unit is only partly destroyed and cannot be lived in, the tenant may choose to end or continue the lease depending on the circumstances, and should get legal advice from an attorney before stopping rent payments. Every situation is different.

14.label: FEMA rental assistance
14.title: FEMA, apply for rental assistance after the Los Angeles County wildfires
14.notes: FEMA may help with temporary housing if a homeowner or renter is displaced from their primary residence by the Los Angeles County wildfires. Transitional Sheltering Assistance gives short-term hotel stays. Rental Assistance continues help afterward and can cover monthly rent, which may include a security deposit. You must show an ongoing need and keep rent receipts for three years. Apply at DisasterAssistance.gov, with the FEMA app, by phone at 800-621-3362, or at a Disaster Recovery Center. The original application deadline for the January 2025 fires has passed, so ask FEMA whether you can still apply or appeal.

15.label: CDI renters guide
15.title: California Department of Insurance, residential insurance guide for homeowners and renters
15.notes: A renters policy covers your own belongings (personal property) and loss of use, plus liability and medical payments to others. Your landlord’s insurance does not cover your belongings. Loss of use on a renters policy is commonly about 20% of the personal property limit. When setting a belongings limit, include everyday items such as small appliances, kitchen items, linens, window coverings, clothing and shoes.

16.label: CDI top ten tips
16.title: California Department of Insurance, Top Ten Tips for Wildfire Claimants
16.notes: Ask your agent or insurer to explain how much coverage you have to rebuild or repair, for belongings and for living expenses, and how to claim those benefits. Keep a dedicated claim diary of every conversation with your insurer or adjuster about the claim and your policy limits. If an adjuster says something is excluded, limited or has conditions, ask them to point to the specific part of the policy. Get at least one estimate from a licensed contractor, because the insurer's estimate may have errors or miss local costs. Track every extra cost of living away from home. Do not rush decisions about contractors, lawyers or public adjusters. The department hotline is 1-800-927-4357.

17.label: United Policyholders, Speak UP
17.title: United Policyholders, Speak UP: how to communicate with your insurance company
17.notes: Create a paper trail: put everything in writing. After a phone call or an in-person talk, confirm any promise or statement from the insurer's staff with a short follow-up email or letter. Keep a notebook or diary of every communication to track the claim. Assume anything you say or write may end up in the insurer's records, and stay polite even when frustrated. Be proactive: give proof of your losses and ask for what you are owed. On coverage questions, ask the insurer to point to the specific policy section. Start with the adjuster and go up to a supervisor if needed, and ask for a written reply within a set time. Keep letters brief, polite and to the point.

18.label: United Policyholders, what to do next
18.title: United Policyholders, if you lost your home or business in the wildfires, here's what to do next (January 8, 2025)
18.notes: Take photos before any cleanup or debris removal. Start a recovery diary with detailed notes on whom you talked to and when, the numbers you called, and what was said. After every talk with an adjuster, send a follow-up email confirming what was discussed. If an adjuster makes a settlement offer on the spot, get a second opinion from an experienced construction professional and review your policy before accepting. Do not sign documents under pressure. Keep photos of receipts such as hotel bills. Adjusters are often reassigned during a claim.

19.label: United Policyholders, general claim tips
19.title: United Policyholders, general claim tips
19.notes: Get a copy of your full policy and declarations page and check the limits. Keep an insurance claim diary: detailed notes of every conversation, with the names, phone numbers and job titles of the insurer's staff and their supervisors. Set deadlines and confirm agreements in writing. Do not give a recorded or sworn statement until you understand your rights; if asked for a recorded statement, you can record it yourself too. Ask the adjuster for a written scope of work that says what repairs they believe are needed, and have your own contractor review it. You do not have to accept the insurer's contractor or estimate. Find out why before signing any release.

20.label: United Policyholders, smoke and ash
20.title: United Policyholders, smoke and ash damage from a wildfire
20.notes: Smoke damage can be invisible, so proper inspection and testing matter. Take pictures of all visible damage. Take notes during inspections and conversations with adjusters. If you think the insurer has not inspected or tested properly, ask in writing and remind it of its duty to investigate all damage, including damage hidden in carpet or behind drywall. An adjuster not trained in air quality testing is only giving an opinion.

21.label: United Policyholders, partial loss fires
21.title: United Policyholders, insurance claim tips for partial loss fires
21.notes: For a serious loss, the inspection by the insurer's adjuster alone is rarely enough; licensed contractors, structural engineers or a Certified Industrial Hygienist may be needed. A thorough inspection covers the roof, stucco and siding, windows, plumbing, heating and ducts, and interior walls and framing. If you or someone in the home has allergies or asthma, tell the adjuster right away.

22.label: United Policyholders, 7 tips
22.title: United Policyholders, insurance claims are a negotiation: 7 tips for Californians who lost homes in fires (January 10, 2025)
22.notes: Treat the claim as a negotiation: ask questions and keep receipts. When it is safe to return, document as much as possible with photos and video of what is left; past photos of the home help you remember what you had. Get estimates from licensed contractors. Do not accept a first settlement without review or rush big financial decisions.

23.label: United Policyholders, Ask an Expert
23.title: United Policyholders, Ask an Expert
23.notes: United Policyholders is a nonprofit for insurance consumers. Its Ask an Expert page is a free public question board where staff and volunteer experts answer insurance claim questions. You need to sign up to post. It does not list a helpline phone number.

24.title: The After Collective, recovery coach

24.notes: The After Collective offers a recovery coach for people rebuilding after a wildfire.

25.label: SAMHSA, 988 Lifeline
25.title: SAMHSA, 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline frequently asked questions
25.notes: The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is free, confidential and open 24/7. You can call or text 988, or chat online. It is not only for suicidal thoughts: people reach out for emotional distress, stress, anxiety and other mental health concerns, or when they are worried about someone else. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911.
